entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 2 1Ti 2:1-15 . Public Worship. Direction as to Intercessions for All Men, since Christ Is a Ransom for All. The Duties of Men and Women Respectively in Respect to Public Prayer. Woman's Subjection; Her Sphere of Duty. 1. therefore-- taking up again the general subject of the Epistle in continuation ( 2Ti 2:1 ). "What I have therefore to say to thee by way of a charge ( 1Ti 1:3 , 18 ), is," &c. that, first of all ... be made-- Alford takes it, "I exhort first of all to make." "First of all," doubtless, is to be connected with "I exhort"; what I begin with (for special reasons), is ... As the destruction of Jerusalem drew near, the Jews (including those at Ephesus) were seized with the dream of freedom from every yoke; and so virtually "'blasphemed" (compare 1Ti 1:20 ) God's name by "speaking evil of dignities" ( 1Ti 6:1 ; 2Pe 2:10 ; Jude 8). Hence Paul, in opposition, gives prominence to the injunction that prayer be made for all men, especially for magistrates and kings ( Tit 3:1-3 ) [Olshausen]. Some professing Christians looked down on all not Christians, as doomed to perdition; but Paul says all men are to be prayed for, as Christ died for all ( 1Ti 2:4-6 ). supplications-- a term implying the suppliant's sense of need, and of his own insufficiency. prayers-- implying devotion. intercessions-- properly the coming near to God with childlike confidence, generally in behalf of another. The accumulation of terms implies prayer in its every form and aspect, according to all the relations implied in it.

For kings--</hi>an effectual confutation of the adversaries who accused the Christians of disaffection to the ruling powers (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.7">Ac 17:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1-Rom.13.7">Ro 13:1-7</reference>).<div eID="gen37164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... in authority--</hi>literally, "in eminence"; in stations of eminence. The "quiet" of Christians was often more dependent on subordinate rulers, than on the supreme king; hence, "all ... in authority" are to be prayed for.<div eID="gen37165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we may lead--</hi>that we may be blessed with such good government as to lead ... ; or rather, as Greek, "to pass" or "spend." The prayers of Christians for the government bring down from heaven peace and order in a state.<div eID="gen37166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">quiet--</hi>not troubled from without.<div eID="gen37167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37168" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peaceable--</hi>"tranquil"; not troubled from within [Olshausen]. "He is peaceable (Greek) who makes no disturbance; he is quiet (Greek) who is himself free from disturbance" [Tittmann].<div eID="gen37168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all godliness--</hi>"in all (possible ... requisite) piety" [Alford]. As "piety" is in relation to God, "gravity" is propriety of behavior among men. In the Old Testament the Jews were commanded to pray for their heathen rulers (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.10">Ezr 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.7">Jr 29:7</reference>). The Jews, by Augustus' order, offered a lamb daily for the Roman emperor, till near the destruction of Jerusalem. The Jewish Zealots, instigated by Eleazar, caused this custom to cease [Josephus, Wars of the Jews, 2.17], whence the war originated, according to Josephus. <div eID="gen37170" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18078"/><div sID="gen37171" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18078"/><hi type="bold">3. this--</hi>praying for all men.<div eID="gen37171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the sight of God--</hi>not merely before men, as if it were their favor that we sought (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.21">2Co 8:21</reference>).<div eID="gen37172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our Saviour--</hi>a title appropriate to the matter in hand. He who is "our Saviour" is willing that all should be saved (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1Ti 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.18">Ro 5:18</reference>); therefore we should meet the will of God in behalf of others, by praying for the salvation of all men. More would be converted if we would pray more. He has actually saved us who believe, being "our Saviour." He is willing that all should be saved, even those who do not as yet believe, if they will believe (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.10">1Ti 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.11">Tit 2:11</reference>). <div eID="gen37173" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18079"/><div sID="gen37174" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18079"/>4. "Imitate God." Since He wishes that all should be saved, do you also wish it; and if you wish it, pray for it. For prayer is the instrument of effecting such things [Chrysostom]. Paul does not say, "He wishes to save all"; for then he would have saved all in matter of fact; but "will have all men to be saved," implies the possibility of man's accepting it (through God's prevenient grace) or rejecting it (through man's own perversity). Our prayers ought to include all, as God's grace included all.<div eID="gen37174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to come--</hi>They are not forced.<div eID="gen37175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the knowledge--</hi>Greek, "the full knowledge" or "recognition" (See on <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">1Co 13:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.9">Php 1:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the truth--</hi>the saving truth as it is in, and by, Jesus (<reference osisRef="John.17.3">Joh 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen37177" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18080"/><div sID="gen37178" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18080"/><hi type="bold">5. For there is one God--</hi>God's unity in essence and purpose is a proof of His comprehending all His human children alike (created in His image) in His offer of grace (compare the same argument from His unity, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.30">Ro 3:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.20">Ga 3:20</reference>); therefore all are to be prayed for. <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1Ti 2:4</reference> is proved from <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">1Ti 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1">1Ti 2:1</reference>, from <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1Ti 2:4</reference>. The one God is common to all (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.22">Is 45:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.26">Ac 17:26</reference>). The one Mediator is mediator between God and all men potentially (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.29">Ro 3:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.5">Ep 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.8.6">He 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.15">9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.24">12:24</reference>). They who have not this one God by one Mediator, have none: literally, a "go-between." The Greek order is not "and one mediator," but "one mediator also between ... While God will have all men to be saved by knowing God and the Mediator, there is a legitimate, holy order in the exercise of that will wherewith men ought to receive it. All mankind constitute, as it were, ONE MAN before God [Bengel].<div eID="gen37178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the man--</hi>rather "man," absolutely and genetically: not a mere individual man: the Second Head of humanity, representing and embodying in Himself the whole human race and nature. There is no "the" in the Greek. This epithet is thus the strongest corroboration of his argument, namely, that Christ's mediation affects the whole race, since there is but the one Mediator, designed as the Representative Man for all men alike (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.5.15">Ro 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.6">1Co 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2Co 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.14">Col 2:14</reference>). His being "man" was necessary to His being a Mediator, sympathizing with us through experimental knowledge of our nature (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Is 50:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.15">4:15</reference>). Even in nature, almost all blessings are conveyed to us from God, not immediately, but through the mediation of various agents. The effectual intercession of Moses for Israel (<reference osisRef="Num.14.13-Num.14.19">Nu 14:13-19</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.9.1-Deut.9.29">De 9:1-29</reference>); of Abraham for Abimelech (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Ge 20:7</reference>); of Job for his friends (<reference osisRef="Job.42.10">Job 42:10</reference>), the mediation being PRESCRIBED by God while declaring His purposes of forgiveness: all prefigure the grand mediation for all by the one Mediator. On the other hand, <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference> asserts that He was also God. <div eID="gen37179" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18081"/><div sID="gen37180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18081"/><hi type="bold">6. gave himself--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit 2:14</reference>). Not only the Father gave Him for us (<reference osisRef="John.3.16">Joh 3:16</reference>); but the Son gave Himself (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.5-Phil.2.8">Php 2:5-8</reference>).<div eID="gen37180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ransom--</hi>properly of a captive slave. Man was the captive slave of Satan, sold under sin. He was unable to ransom himself, because absolute obedience is due to God, and therefore no act of ours can satisfy for the least offense. <reference osisRef="Lev.25.48">Le 25:48</reference> allowed one sold captive to be redeemed by one of his brethren. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18089"/><div sID="gen37208" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18089"/><hi type="bold">14. Adam was not deceived--</hi>as Eve was deceived by the serpent; but was persuaded by his wife. <reference osisRef="Gen.3.17">Ge 3:17</reference>, "hearkened unto ... voice of ... wife." But in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.13">Ge 3:13</reference>, Eve says, "The serpent beguiled me." Being more easily deceived, she more easily deceives [Bengel], (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.3">2Co 11:3</reference>). Last in being, she was first in sin--indeed, she alone was deceived. The subtle serpent knew that she was "the weaker vessel" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.7">1Pe 3:7</reference>). He therefore tempted her, not Adam. She yielded to the temptations of sense and the deceits of Satan; he, to conjugal love. Hence, in the order of God's judicial sentence, the serpent, the prime offender, stands first; the woman, who was deceived, next; and the man, persuaded by his wife, last (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.14-Gen.3.19">Ge 3:14-19</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Rom.5.12">Ro 5:12</reference>, Adam is represented as the first transgressor; but there no reference is made to Eve, and Adam is regarded as the head of the sinning race. Hence, as here, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>, in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Ge 3:16</reference>, woman's "subjection" is represented as the consequence of her being deceived.<div eID="gen37208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37209" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being deceived--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read the compound Greek verb for the simple, "Having been seduced by deceit": implying how completely Satan succeeded in deceiving her.<div eID="gen37209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37210" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was in the transgression--</hi>Greek, "came to be in the transgression": became involved in the existing state of transgression, literally, "the going beyond a command"; breach of a positive precept (<reference osisRef="Rom.4.15">Ro 4:15</reference>). <div eID="gen37210" type="x-p"/>

But in Ge 3:13 , Eve says, "The serpent beguiled me." Being more easily deceived, she more easily deceives [Bengel], ( 2Co 11:3 ). Last in being, she was first in sin--indeed, she alone was deceived. Hence, in the order of God's judicial sentence, the serpent, the prime offender, stands first; the woman, who was deceived, next; and the man, persuaded by his wife, last ( Ge 3:14-19 ). In Ro 5:12 , Adam is represented as the first transgressor; but there no reference is made to Eve, and Adam is regarded as the head of the sinning race. Hence, as here, 1Ti 2:11 , in Ge 3:16 , woman's "subjection" is represented as the consequence of her being deceived. being deceived-- The oldest manuscripts read the compound Greek verb for the simple, "Having been seduced by deceit": implying how completely Satan succeeded in deceiving her. was in the transgression-- Greek, "came to be in the transgression": became involved in the existing state of transgression, literally, "the going beyond a command"; breach of a positive precept ( Ro 4:15 ).
